newsitem.title: USA: Brady debt surges on delayed reaction to Fed.
newsitem.headline: Brady debt surges on delayed reaction to Fed.

text.p: Taking a cue from U.S. Treasury bonds, emerging market debt prices soared Wednesday as players adjusted to the Federal Reserve's decision Tuesday to hold U.S. interest rates steady, traders said.

The delayed reaction to the Fed jolted several Brady bonds prices to their highest levels this year. Fixed-rate Brady instruments surged as investors adjusted to prospects of steady U.S. rates for at least six weeks.
"You have two factors: the delayed rally in the U.S. bond and the liquidity from people who are sittiing on cash and need toget invested," one Brady trader said.
Argentine Pars gained one point to 58-3/8 and Venezuelan pars stormed 1-3/8 to 68-3/4.
Brazilian Cs leading the charge with a stunning 1-3/8 move higher to 75-1/2.
"You did not have a driver that was purely Brazilian," said another trader at a U.S. money center bank. "It was an emerging markets story." 23/32 to yield 6.93 percent.
The drive skywards was propelled by a short squeeze that occurred when some players sought to sell into strength and then found the market determined to hold long positions.
"The long bond yields were falling and that put a little pressure on the heels of the short guys to rush to cover the positions," said Marcelo Fleury, vice president at Garband Corporates.
The key question will be whether the market can maintain its current levels, dealers said.
Prices could well be supported if institutional investment continues tp flow into the emerging market at its record levels, but some traders cautioned that a correction may be ahead.
"I would be very cautious at coming in at these levels," Fleury said. "We might see Bradies trading in a very narrow range between now and the next FOMC meeting (November 13)."

Lipper Analytical Services announced that emerging market bond funds have returned an average of about 28 percent in the year to date, while the average U.S. equity fund has gained 12.36 percent, the average taxable bond fund 0.95 percent, and the general municipal debt fund is off 0.59 percent.
Some of those stunning gains were propelled by massive returns on Russian debt, which has slumped recently amid concerns over the health of Russian president Boris Yeltsin.
On Wednesday, Russian Vnesh dollar-denominated paper gained two points to 65-1/2.

Peter Allen, Bank of Boston's chief of research, said in a paper that Russian debt had potential for additional price appreciation, ahead of reduced Vnesh deal risk and a likely year-end closing, a favorable inaugural Eurobond slated for October/November and the IMF program back on track.
